objectives: Describe the three energy systems (ATP-PCr, anaerobic glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation) and their characteristic time courses.
Relate energy-system contribution to exercise duration and explain the lactate threshold.
Interpret the respiratory exchange ratio and excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC).

slides.title: ATP and the three energy systems
slides.body:
Every muscular contraction is paid for in the same currency: **adenosine triphosphate**, or **ATP**. When a myosin head splits ATP into **ADP** (adenosine diphosphate) and inorganic phosphate, it releases the free energy that drives the cross-bridge cycle. The energy of hydrolysis is large, roughly $-30.5\ \text{kJ/mol}$ under standard conditions and even more under cellular conditions. The catch is that muscle stores only a tiny amount of ATP, enough for a second or two of all-out effort. To keep contracting, the cell must regenerate ATP continuously, and it has three systems to do so.

The **first system** is the **phosphocreatine system**, also called the **ATP-PCr** or **phosphagen** system. Muscle stores **phosphocreatine** (PCr, also called creatine phosphate), a high-energy molecule that can rapidly donate its phosphate to ADP. The reaction, catalyzed by the enzyme **creatine kinase**, is

$$\text{PCr} + \text{ADP} \rightarrow \text{ATP} + \text{creatine}$$

This is essentially instantaneous and oxygen-independent, but stores are small, so it powers only about the first **10 seconds** of maximal effort. It dominates a shot put, a single heavy lift, or the start of a sprint.

The **second system** is **anaerobic glycolysis**, the breakdown of **glucose** or stored **glycogen** to **pyruvate** without oxygen. The pathway, worked out by **Gustav Embden**, **Otto Meyerhof**, and **Jakub Parnas** (the **Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway**), yields a net of 2 ATP per glucose and, when fast, produces **lactate**. This system supplies high power for roughly **10 seconds to 2 minutes**, fueling efforts such as a 400 m run.

The **third system** is **oxidative phosphorylation**, the **aerobic** pathway. Pyruvate enters the **mitochondria**, is converted to **acetyl-CoA**, and is oxidized through the **citric acid cycle** (the Krebs cycle, named for **Hans Krebs**) and the **electron transport chain**. With oxygen, full oxidation of one glucose yields on the order of 30 to 32 ATP, and fats yield far more per molecule. This system is slow to ramp up but essentially limitless in duration, powering everything from rest to a marathon.

These three systems are always running together; what changes is their relative contribution, which depends overwhelmingly on the intensity and duration of the effort.

slides.title: Energy-system contribution as a function of duration
slides.body:
No single energy system switches cleanly on or off. Instead, the **relative contribution** of the three systems shifts continuously as an effort lengthens. Understanding this curve is the heart of training design.

For a maximal effort, the pattern is approximately:

- In the first **few seconds**, the **ATP-PCr system** supplies the overwhelming majority of energy because it is the fastest to respond.
- From about **10 seconds to 2 minutes**, **anaerobic glycolysis** becomes the dominant contributor, producing ATP quickly but accumulating **lactate** and hydrogen ions.
- Beyond about **2 minutes**, **oxidative phosphorylation** takes over and becomes the principal source for any sustained effort.

A useful landmark is that around the **1 to 2 minute** mark, the aerobic and anaerobic contributions to a maximal effort are roughly equal; this **crossover** is why an 800 m run is famously brutal, drawing heavily on both systems at once.

Duration alone does not tell the whole story. Even at rest the **aerobic system** dominates, fueled mostly by **fat oxidation**. As intensity climbs from easy to hard, two things happen: total energy demand rises, and the **fuel mix** shifts from fat toward carbohydrate because carbohydrate yields more ATP per litre of oxygen.

A classic illustration is the relationship between exercise intensity and the source of fuel. At low intensities fat provides most of the energy; at high intensities carbohydrate dominates because glycolytic flux is high and fat oxidation cannot keep pace. The intensity at which fat oxidation peaks in absolute terms is sometimes called **FATmax** and is of interest to endurance coaches.

The practical upshot is that an event's duration and intensity dictate which energy system to train. A powerlifter trains the **phosphagen** system with brief maximal efforts and long rests. A 400 m runner trains **glycolytic** capacity and lactate tolerance. A marathoner trains **oxidative** capacity, mitochondrial density, and fat oxidation. Because the systems overlap, almost every athlete trains all three to some degree, but the emphasis follows the bioenergetic demands of the sport. This logic traces directly back to the lactic-acid and oxygen-debt experiments of **A.V. Hill** and **Otto Meyerhof** in the 1920s.

slides.title: Lactate threshold, EPOC, and the respiratory exchange ratio
slides.body:
Three measurable concepts let scientists read the energy systems from outside the body.

The **lactate threshold** is the exercise intensity above which blood **lactate** begins to accumulate faster than it can be cleared. At low intensity, lactate produced by glycolysis is shuttled to other tissues and oxidized (the **lactate shuttle** described by **George Brooks**), so blood lactate stays near baseline. As intensity rises past the threshold, production outstrips clearance and lactate climbs sharply. A common reference point is the **onset of blood lactate accumulation (OBLA)** near $4\ \text{mmol/L}$. Crucially, modern physiology rejects the old idea that lactate itself causes fatigue or muscle soreness; lactate is a usable fuel, and the accumulating hydrogen ions, not lactate, contribute to the acidosis. The lactate threshold is one of the best predictors of endurance performance, often better than $\dot{V}O_2max$ alone, because it marks the highest intensity an athlete can sustain.

**Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption**, or **EPOC**, is the elevated oxygen uptake that persists after exercise stops. Historically **A.V. Hill** called the early portion the **oxygen debt**. EPOC reflects the metabolic cost of restoring the body to rest: replenishing **ATP** and **phosphocreatine**, re-oxygenating **myoglobin** and **hemoglobin**, clearing metabolites, and supporting elevated temperature, heart rate, and ventilation. High-intensity exercise produces a larger and longer EPOC than steady moderate exercise, which is part of why interval training is metabolically expensive.

The **respiratory exchange ratio**, or **RER**, is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed, measured at the mouth:

$$RER = \frac{\dot{V}CO_2}{\dot{V}O_2}$$

It reveals the fuel mix. Oxidizing pure **carbohydrate** gives $RER = 1.0$, because the stoichiometry produces one molecule of $CO_2$ per molecule of $O_2$ consumed. Oxidizing pure **fat** gives $RER \approx 0.7$, since fat oxidation consumes relatively more oxygen. A resting value near $0.8$ indicates a mixed diet. During increasing exercise intensity the RER rises toward and may even exceed $1.0$, the latter signaling that **carbon dioxide** is being driven off by buffering of lactic acidosis rather than pure substrate oxidation. Together, the lactate threshold, EPOC, and RER let a sport scientist infer which energy systems an athlete is using without ever taking a muscle biopsy, making them everyday tools in the performance laboratory.

question.question: An athlete performs an all-out effort lasting about 8 seconds (a single maximal sprint start). Which energy system supplies the majority of ATP?
options: Oxidative phosphorylation, because it produces the most ATP per glucose.
Anaerobic glycolysis, because lactate is needed immediately.
The ATP-PCr (phosphagen) system, because it regenerates ATP fastest and dominates the first ~10 seconds.
Fat oxidation, because it is the default fuel at rest.
question.explanation: The ATP-PCr system uses creatine kinase to regenerate ATP from phosphocreatine almost instantaneously and without oxygen. Its stores are small, so it dominates only the first ~10 seconds of maximal effort, which covers an 8-second sprint start. Glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation become dominant over longer durations.

hints: Which system is the fastest to respond, regardless of total yield?
Think about the ~10 second time window of the phosphagen system.
slides.workedSolution: An 8-second maximal effort falls inside the roughly 10-second window where phosphocreatine, via creatine kinase, regenerates ATP faster than any other route and without needing oxygen. Although oxidative phosphorylation yields far more ATP per glucose, it is too slow to dominate such a brief, explosive bout. Therefore the ATP-PCr system is the primary supplier and the third option is correct.

question.question: During steady-state exercise an athlete consumes oxygen at $\dot{V}O_2 = 3.0\ \text{L/min}$ and produces carbon dioxide at $\dot{V}CO_2 = 2.7\ \text{L/min}$. Compute the respiratory exchange ratio (RER). Give a decimal.
An RER value of approximately what number indicates that the athlete is oxidizing almost entirely fat? Give the decimal value to two significant figures.
question.hint: Pure carbohydrate oxidation gives 1.0; pure fat gives a lower value near 0.7.

question.question: Design energy-system training for an 800 m runner.
question.prompt: You are working with an 800 m runner whose event lasts roughly two minutes. Using the time course of the three energy systems, explain why this event sits almost exactly at the crossover where aerobic and anaerobic contributions are nearly equal. Recommend how you would balance training between glycolytic (lactate-tolerance) sessions and aerobic (oxidative-capacity) sessions, and explain how you would use the athlete's lactate threshold to monitor whether the aerobic base is improving over a season.

question.question: Which statement about lactate during exercise reflects the modern (post-1980s) understanding?
options: Lactate is the direct cause of delayed muscle soreness and must be flushed out by stretching.
Lactate is a metabolic dead-end waste product that the body cannot reuse.
Lactate is a usable fuel that can be shuttled to and oxidized by other tissues, and the associated acidosis is driven by hydrogen ions rather than lactate itself.
Lactate accumulation has no relationship to endurance performance.
question.explanation: Following George Brooks's work on the lactate shuttle, lactate is recognized as a valuable fuel that is transported to and oxidized by the heart, slow-twitch fibers, and other tissues. The fatigue and acidosis once blamed on lactate are attributable mainly to hydrogen-ion accumulation. The lactate threshold remains a strong predictor of endurance performance, so the other options are outdated or wrong.

hints: Distinguish lactate the molecule from the hydrogen ions that cause acidosis.
slides.workedSolution: The lactate shuttle, described by George Brooks, established that lactate is actively transported to other tissues and oxidized as fuel rather than being a dead-end waste product. The acidosis of intense exercise stems from hydrogen-ion accumulation, not from lactate per se, and lactate is not the cause of delayed-onset soreness. Because the lactate threshold strongly predicts endurance capacity, only the third option matches current understanding.
